title: Guard the mind
hook: a list of resolutions broken by noon; Shantideva says guard one thing, the mind, and the rest are kept
carry: guard the mind with the rope of mindfulness
tomorrow: nobody can cover the whole earth in leather. so what can you do?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed chapter four with a search: where would they go? Look straight at an urge, ask where it would live, and it has no home. Chapter five opens with the guard who does the looking.
screen: `WHERE WOULD IT LIVE?` → `CHAPTER FIVE: THE GUARD.`

segments.voice: No phone at dinner. No snacks after nine. Be kinder to your brother. Drink more water. Answer emails the same day. A list of good rules taped to the fridge, and by noon on Monday half of them are already broken. Each rule needs its own guard, and there aren't enough guards. So, yesterday's question: is there one guard that keeps them all? Shantideva says yes, and he puts it in the very first verse of his new chapter.
screen: `A LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `BROKEN BY NOON.` → `ONE GUARD FOR ALL?`

segments.voice: Whoever wants to guard their training, he says, must guard the mind with great care; let the mind go unguarded, and the training can't be kept. Then a picture. An untamed mind is like a wild elephant, doing more harm than any elephant in a rage. But tie that elephant with the rope of mindfulness, and fears fall away and good things follow. So the one guard is attention itself, checking in: where is my mind right now, and what is it about to do? Neighbors know this teaching. The book of Proverbs, in the Jewish and Christian Bible, says in the King James English: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Shared ground, and plenty of it: both put the inner life first, upstream of every rule, and both say keeping it takes steady effort. One honest difference. In Proverbs, a parent hands down wisdom that begins, as the book says, in the fear of the LORD; the heart is kept by holding to God's teaching. Shantideva's guard is the mind watching itself, mindfulness and alertness, with no creator giving the command. One heart, one mind, kept with care.
screen: `GUARD THE MIND, KEEP THE TRAINING.` · `THE ELEPHANT AND THE ROPE.` · `KEEP THY HEART WITH ALL DILIGENCE.` · `SHARED CARE, DIFFERENT KEEPERS.` · then, large: `GUARD THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one steady sound around you: a fan, traffic, the hum of a fridge. Rest your listening there. Each time you notice you've drifted somewhere else, simply ask, where is my mind right now, and come back to the sound. That checking-in is the guard.
Guard the mind: chapter five's first teaching. Keep watch over the mind, and every other promise has a keeper.
One line for the road: guard the mind with the rope of mindfulness, and the rules mostly look after themselves. Day one of chapter five.

howItsDone: Buddhists train mindfulness (smriti) and alertness (samprajanya) in sitting meditation and through the day, often by pausing to check what the mind is doing; Shantideva's fifth chapter is studied as a guide to that watchfulness.

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): shared with Jewish and Christian neighbors, the inner life kept first and with effort, in Proverbs' own words (Proverbs 4:23, KJV). Honest difference: in Proverbs the heart is kept by holding to a parent's God-given wisdom (Proverbs 1:7, paraphrased); Shantideva's guard is mindfulness and alertness, with no creator commanding it. No ranking, no 'the same'. Please confirm both sides are fairly stated, ideally with a Jewish and a Christian reader.
5.1-5.3 paraphrased: guard the mind to guard the training; the mad elephant; the rope of mindfulness. Confirm verse numbers.
Chapter 5's Sanskrit title is samprajanya-rakshana (guarding alertness); the outline calls the chapter 'Watchfulness'.
Gloss 'LORD': the KJV small-capitals LORD renders the divine name; the lesson's spoken line says 'as the book says, in the fear of the LORD'. Confirm a Jewish reviewer is comfortable with this gloss.
